content:
I'm in the following situation: Myself and a collaborator have proved an open conjecture with the heavy use of AI and Lean (using personal Claude subscriptions we paid for out of our own pockets). It took us about a week. The proof of this conjecture would normally constitute an academic paper, and the proof of similar results has. The lean code itself takes ~a day to build, not because it is large but it is computationally very heavy (lots of decide). But despite knowing the statement of this conjecture very well, the proof uses techniques that are beyond my area of research, and I do not fully understand them.

The Lean code currently sits in a private repo, and I am deliberately not saying what the conjecture is (although it's not too exciting). This is mainly because of the recent discussions about AI, Lean and mathematics, and I want to make sure we do things in the right way here. So I want to ask, what do we do next to disseminate this proof or the fact we have a proof, so that we do it in the 'right way'?

Not entirely sure either, but I have asked myself similar questions lately. Having a look at criteria for authorship (see ours at the University of Melbourne) is useful as it helps determining whether you can scientifically claim this as your own work (and notably whether you can publish this). But if this is not the case, e.g. if you haven't prompted in an insightful enough way the LLM (in my experience, they can solve problems without being guided by an expert), then I really do not know how to communicate this kind of result. So, I am happy to follow this conversation to see what others have to say about this! :slight_smile:
Have you added to human understanding beyond ticking a box saying "this conjecture is true"? Do you now know "why" it's true, for example?
Not at this stage, no. By which I mean, if I was invited to give a talk, and asked just to talk about the mathematics of the proof (not the Lean), I could not do it.
Then it sounds like anyone can prove the conjecture themselves for $200 and achieve all you have achieved?

You may want to leave a public trail of the Lean formalization that can stand later audit, at the earliest possible time.

But the infrastructure support seems to be lacking: Palomar currently only supports public repos if you wish to keep the repo private for now; lean-eval supports private submissions but only for publicly stated problems so yours may not be on it, it has public metadata record such as author, timestamp and commit hash, see here for an example of private submission; only a private repo that turns public later doesn't stand audit because timestamps and other metadata of git history can be easily overwritten.
What about publishing just the commit hash without the actual repo?

Kevin Buzzard said:

Then it sounds like anyone can prove the conjecture themselves for $200 and achieve all you have achieved?

For the sake of argument - I think the answer to this is likely yes. I think the one could argue that knowing that this was a conjecture which could likely be solved now, with the current capabilities of AI, and how to prompt the AI to get to a solution in Lean was likely our only input here.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Then it sounds like anyone can prove the conjecture themselves for $200 and achieve all you have achieved?

I have a few mechanisations which are of this nature, where I know the statement, I can know of the area, but I do not have a deep (or any, in some cases) understanding of the proof. Yet, I feel like the community could benefit from having access to the mechanisation of these results, to inspect it at least and therefore get a sense of confidence about the results (some of the results I had mechanised are somewhat controversial). But even in this case, without intention of claiming any kind of authorship, I am not sure how to communicate these results.

I actually would prefer to make the repo public. The only reason I haven't yet, is because I want to make sure that this is what the community thinks is best to do in this case.

Regarding Palomer and lean-eval, I'm not sure in this specific case they would accept the repo. A naive lake build blows up memory so the files have to be built in a specific (non-parallel) way. But I think this is a detail we can ignore right now.
Have you checked that the Lean definitions and theorem statements are correct, i.e., capture what was intended?
Yes, this is the sort of problem where the definitions involved and the statement of the theorem are very simple to state (high-school level maths), so are easy to check

I guess then this is a datapoint: "in September 2026 you can solve Navier-Stokes with something like $15M but you can solve this conjecture with $200." Write a good #formalization.yaml file, check the conjecture is not already solved and then submit it to lean-eval if it's on there and Palomar if it's not, and we can have what sounds like the more interesting discussion of how your proof breaks their system and whether this means their system needs fixing. I would imagine that the maintainers of these systems want to understand how to scale.

So I think this solves part of the problem: How to disseminate the proof to the Lean community:

  1. Put it in a public repo.
  2. Add a good #formalization.yaml.
  3. Submit to lean-eval or Palomar.

But then there is the question of how to disseminate this to the wider Mathematics community. Here is one idea:

  1. Create a public thread on this Zulip about 'digesting' the Lean proof.
  2. Invite anyone to take part in that.
  3. Once a valid digest has taken place, invite all those who made a substantial contribution to join in writing a paper on it. "The formalization and digest of the proof of ..."

What do people think about this? Is this the sort of thing we would want to see.
I think there is a bit of a digestion backlog right now in mathematics, because results are being released 100x as fast as usual.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

But then there is the question of how to disseminate this to the wider Mathematics community.

If it passes Palomar and it resolves an open problem, submit to vibemathed.com .

Do you know any colleagues who are expert of the field or tools uses by the proof, and would be able to help you with understanding and disseminating it? Or anyone you could reach out to? It is quite normal to add someone to a collaboration when you lack expertise in one specific part of it. I am not sure how it translates to this new world, but I would imagine having someone interested in the conjecture write a good quality presentation of the proof would add a lot of value (if you are willing to invest the time).

For digestion, I would recommend:

  • Try to understand the proof yourself, use your Claude for it. Look for a better way (the first proof often is not the best one).
  • If there will be other people interested in the math behind the proof (I don't know how much public interest this conjecture has), privately offer them an access to a chatbot which knows the proof, and is able to interact with the Lean files (so that it is grounded). Your Claude could have some ideas how to set this up.

There are cases where people feed their unpublished drafts containing novel ideas to AI, which end up working and verified in Lean because AI used "techniques that are beyond their area of research" to overcome the difficulties that they could not overcome themselves, and they don't even have the clues on which area of experts to talk to before obtaining the AI output, and possibly even after. That seems to be a legitimate use of AI models in a research capacity.

In this case, their novel ideas and AI's "substantial contribution of knowledge that influences the research and its output" per clause 5.2.c may share coauthorship. Now, they may choose to privately reach out to experts with clues on who to talk to, and later author an academic paper together after proper mathematical development and exposition. But that may takes months, and the model release cycle or some rumor-based scoop may predate that, especially if they forgot to turn some "training on data" switch off or the switch didn't work. That is a true dilemma in this era.

In this case, it is best to leave a public trail of the Lean formalization of the full result first, while optionally keep the content private for the time being. Then they may choose to publish or go public with their novel draft and claim on only that part, the rest are considered as public domain knowledge to archive.

Or, they may also choose to go through proper mathematical development and exposition as above, but they will have the public trail to (partly) support any claims later. Chances are, there would be concurrent work, or sources not known to the authors were used to produce the AI output, then an update to attributions is in order.

Max Nowak 🐉 said:

What about publishing just the commit hash without the actual repo?

... or publish an encrypted archive of git repo, with key to be announced

There are people who are interested in this conjecture (I believe), and there are people we could reach out to help write a good exposition of the proof.

But the general philosophy of: Making the Lean result public now, and disseminating a (human) digest of the proof at a later date (either with extra co-authors or having spent time digesting ourselves), seems to be the way to go? What about social media posts + blog posts? Where do these fit in?

I'm slightly worried here that we essentially just fall into the same pattern as OpenAI and Navier-Stokes. Although I would be surprised if there were people actively working on it now, its not impossible, and I don't know everything Claude has been trained on.
For sake of completeness here is the commit hash :): 2b54de4aeb01a65197f7e7e2227860f957258da7

I am a bit surprised by these suggestions because I thought the standard we were advocating for was to join a lean formalisation with a human written article, which motivates the results and describes the ideas of the proof. It has always been the case that articles take time - so far, both the proof and exposition would take time, but now this should be much faster when you don't have to produce a rigid mathematical explanation. Maybe I am being too idealistic here.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

I'm slightly worried here that we essentially just fall into the same pattern as OpenAI and Navier-Stokes.

I think one of the biggest problems with OpenAI's pattern is that they (probably) won't make a digested output. What has been suggested here is to announce the result and share Lean code, and later make a good human-readable explanation of it. It seems to me that (ignoring the Lean code part) this has been common mathematical practice, so I'd argue this is fine.

@Joseph Tooby-Smith Is there any need to rush to announce soon? Are you interested in spending some time and energy to understand the proof better? If not, are you willing to forgo credits, because you seem to say you only did a bit of prompting?
@Johan Commelin Conversely, is there any reason not to rush (so long as a digested proof is later presented)? Obviously, rushing gives you academic credits.

It is quite common in old school academia to have to sit for months / years on a new proof because it takes times to tick all the boxes to reach credit. I am concerned that giving out credit at the formalisation stage and allowing for later explanations of the work will just lead to no explanations in a lot of cases. To me it feels like if you "just" get a blacl box lean proof that you don't understand there is not much credit to claim until it is explained - for OpenAI or ourselves.

Fernando Chu said:

Johan Commelin Conversely, is there any reason not to rush (so long as a digested proof is later presented)? Obviously, rushing gives you academic credits.

I don't think "I pushed a button" gives you any academic credit. Edit: sorry, that's exactly what Laura just said!

I agree with @Laura Monk 's comment here. For what its worth, we also don't think we should get academic credit for this (or at least what we have done so far), but: this was an open problem, it is of interest to some people (has a wikipedia page etc), and we now know it to be true and have a formal proof. To us (myself and @Alex Zughaid - who is a student and my collaborator on this ), this is information which pushes forward the knowledge of community. To not share it, and pretend it doesn't exist also seems to be a disservice.

A good practical reason to sit on a new proof for months / years (privately), is that at least advancing the understanding is still at a similar pace as before, or at least everyone is at the same accelerated rate.

Equally it is not necessarily a bad thing to have public trail first with the intention to go through proper mathematical development and exposition, and tick all the boxes.
To be clear, I don't think it should give academic credit, I do think it currently does, however. E.g., by getting citations, which some hiring committees love.

I think the other thing to consider here is: If we release the proof, but do not give digest of it, it seems unlikely that anyone else will - because our current academic credit system won't reward the person who does this in the same way if they were the ones who produced the proof.

If it has a wikipedia page, who is to say someone else won't just publish it in a few weeks time? I personally don't think it makes sense to make decisions based on an outdated incentive structure, rather than imagining how the system should work. (I don't have a concrete proposal on how it should work or what you should do though!)

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

I think the other thing to consider here is: If we release the proof, but do not give digest of it, it seems unlikely that anyone else will - because our current academic credit system won't reward the person who does this in the same way if they were the ones who produced the proof.

But still, a mathematician working in that field, asking an AI (that has read the Lean on Palomar) for ideas, might do something great(er) with it.

Currently nobody could get credit for situations like this, but some may benefit from it. This discourages the roles acting in good faith, including the ones willing to share the result (even including AI companies although they benefitted from it outside academia), and the ones willing to go through proper mathematical exposition on the result.

So the question here is: if I find a Lean proof of an important conjecture using AI, is it helpful for the researchers interested in the conjecture (or the broader community) to share it? Should we have a special sharing (or even credit) system for this new possibility?

I would argue that, for the researchers in this community to extract anything from a Lean formalisation, they would need to be either proficient in Lean or use AI significantly. In this case, they could also have solved the problem themselves with little effort (it appears). So is there any value for them in sharing this?

Furthermore, we all know people lose motivation once credit is claimed orproof status is recognised. I am not sure there is currently any incentive to work on this once claimed.

Laura Monk said:

I am not sure there is currently any incentive to work on this once claimed.

...if you care more for your ego than for the advancement of the field.

To me, this discussion is a bit weird as we are getting just hints so far which problem it is (like "it has a Wikipedia page"). I would like to ask the people here who think that the Lean proof should not be published soon: Would you consider it problematic to explicitly state here which conjecture it is?

@Joseph Tooby-Smith You should also consider that publishing it without really understanding it it's a bit risky: if people start saying you are only a "button pusher" it will be not so easy to convince them this not the case. Let me stress that I am not saying you are, but here we are talking about reputation, and people are often not very rational or don't have time to dig into the full story.

Ralf Stephan said:

Laura Monk said:

I am not sure there is currently any incentive to work on this once claimed.

...if you care more for your ego than for the advancement of the field.

But there is no guarantee someone ever will. As opposed to if we make it a requirement at the level of claiming the result.

So let the "button pushers" do what they do. The simple button pushers are already losing steam, see the plateau at https://vibemathed.com/stats#over-time. Eventually, only the smart button pushers will remain.

Mirek Olšák said:

To me, this discussion is a bit weird as we are getting just hints so far which problem it is (like "it has a Wikipedia page"). I would like to ask the people here who think that the Lean proof should not be published soon: Would you consider it problematic to explicitly state here which conjecture it is?

Want to highlight this - happy to share the conjecture if people see fit.

Riccardo Brasca said:

Joseph Tooby-Smith You should also consider that publishing it without really understanding it it's a bit risky: if people start saying you are only a "button pusher" it will be not so easy to convince them this not the case. Let me stress that I am not saying you are, but here we are talking about reputation, and people are often not very rational or don't have time to dig into the full story.

Agreed. We certainly would not post anything on e.g. arXiv without understanding things fully.

(Also hopefully clear here that as well as been interested to do in our specific case, I am interested in the broader question of what we do in situations like this, as they will no doubt become more common).

To me, going public claiming a conjecture without a paper to back it is not considered an acceptable academic practice (in the usual/past academic codes). So that would be why. When I proved a conjecture with my collaborator and still spent 1 year writing the paper, we were very careful to never claim it proven (even though people knew we were working on it). Here the line is finer as some people view a lean proof as a full proof, whilst others do not (meaning they require an additional breakdown of a proof). So the question is simply: what is the requirement for going public with a proof? Lean or Lean + article?
@Laura Monk if someone had come out with a proof of that conjecture in the year you spent writing it, what would you have done? Would that change in this new AI world?

It has happened to us with other partial results, in which case we evaluated whether or not we had something ready to share within the few weeks after the competing release. When it was not the case we let it go (but other people did put their alternate proof out 3 weeks later, got credit, and I truely appreciated the input of their article).

This is the problem of conjecture - focused academia. It causes hard races and credit questions, and is quite amplified by AI.
Would it be a big deal for you if someone came out in a little while with a Lean proof + an explanation, given the time invested?
No, but I think it would be an issue if someone came out with a Lean proof without an explanation, and then got a bunch of credit for it; because they just went ahead anyway and did it.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

No, but I think it would be an issue if someone came out with a Lean proof without an explanation, and then got a bunch of credit for it; because they just went ahead anyway and did it.

Indeed but if that were to happen, you'd be able to immediatly release your proof, which would normally indicate you already had it (or would it not?). However doing this yourself, you could be cutting off other people themselves working really hard on a write-up.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

No, but I think it would be an issue if someone came out with a Lean proof without an explanation, and then got a bunch of credit for it; because they just went ahead anyway and did it.

If they hand-wrote the lean proof it shouldn’t be an issue. If it was AI generated it would be an issue. I don’t know where the inflection point is for partially generated proofs. For example if you backfill a basic lemma that mathlib doesn’t have with AI, but isn’t a critical part of the proof (your community believes it and doesn’t care to see an explicit proof of it), I’d still say it is fine.

Is there a difference here between making something "public" vs "publicizing" it? Let's say we want to make it public so that others can look at it, and maybe learn from it; is that different from publicizing it as a proof, or a completed project? (I'm trying to work out how all this fits in with a science-done-openly approach).
Isn't publicizing possibly going to make people who could be working on this have to race against the clock?
Can I ask you @Joseph Tooby-Smith what would be the issue with finding a collaborator with a complementary skill set to write up with? (which is exactly the old way, just with different skills here)
No, this wouldn't be an issue, and is likely the road we will go down.
Well good luck with this: it looks like an exciting project and I am looking forward to hearing more :)

I think my current unease is the following:

We can follow the approach(which is what I think is laid out here): Keep things private (but maybe keep a public trail e.g. commit hashes) until there is a complete digest of the proof, which we can publish in the usual ways. We can advocate for others to do the same.

But this system seems fragile as a whole, since it relies on us doing something active to protect the community here. If we had already made it public, or had done the work publicly from the start (because we wanted it to be a community project), we would not be able to follow this approach. Or if we were actively seeking academic credit we could just publish the result, and move on (which people are actively doing).

My guess is that eventually, the standard becomes: Publish the Lean proof first, understand it later. Personally, I also prefer openness, and there is not enough force in the world to keep the advances hidden. However, academia apparently needs some time to get used to it -- to realize what actually matters, how to adapt... That is why at this moment, being discrete and privately reaching mathematicians to collaborate with sounds like a better strategy (with the main risk being that they might be flooded with similar requests).

Honestly, I find it very likely that if you won't manage to publish the result within a month, someone else will get AI solve the same, and publish it with less caution. But at least, you will have the math community on your side this time :wink:

Academia is not going to change its standards. Solutions of math problems do not matter nearly as much as you seem to think it does, without human understanding and digestion.

edit: based on the confused reactions I ought to clarify : when we solve a problem, it is important to know why or how an approach works and why others fail. For example if someone solved P vs NP, it has to explain why the proof doesn’t relativise or why 3SAT is suddenly so much harder than 2SAT. Just a proof dump we can’t understand doesn’t make any difference. It is an academic’s job to reach this understanding and communicate it. That’s not going to change. Neither is the basic standard for how credit is allocated and the importance of citation.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

you think it does

???

Academia rests on many norms and ethical values we share. We come to an agreement to not steal people's work, to not fake lab results, to not lie. All of these things can be easily broken and have been in the past. The only cost being the loss of academic reputation. We need to update these standards to new developments.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

(I'm trying to work out how all this fits in with a science-done-openly approach).

There are 3 factors in play here: prematurely going public with a Lean formalization and the claims attached to it, gets no credit, negative reputation, and likely has a net negative impact on the resource (experts, funding etc.) to work on the related problems. The practice of open science, rests on there is some science to open.
It is also worth saying that I think this community is actively prompting releasing these sorts of proofs publicly with things like palomar.

Maybe you can think of it this way: you have the opportunity to simultanously prove a significant conjecture, increase our knowledge, AND give a great example of how AI + Lean + us researchers can work together. This is actually a lot to accomplish in one project!

...great example of how AI + Lean + us researchers can work together

I actually think that is the most interesting question here :).

@Shreyas Srinivas
The confusion is coming from you implying that I am giving a truth guarantee too much value, whereas my post was not about it at all. Quite the contrary. My claim is that people do not want to see a truth guarantee about a famous conjecture public because of the discrepancy between a perceived value of a truth guarantee, and the real value of it.
If there was no discrepancy, and everyone understood the real value / non-value of what is published, there would be no reason to hide the fact that a truth guarantee was found, of which conjecture, how the Lean proof looks, etc. That is a world I would like to see, and this is the shift that needs to happen in academia as well.

I just want to say that I appreciate the thoughtful discussion here. I don't have much of an opinion to share myself, but reading this conversation, especially after everything last week, makes me optimistic :blue_heart:

Mirek Olšák said:

If there was no discrepancy, and everyone understood the real value / non-value of what is published, there would be no reason to hide the fact that a truth guarantee was found, of which conjecture, how the Lean proof looks, etc. That is a world I would like to see, and this is the shift that needs to happen in academia as well.

Maybe a question open to everyone: Is there something we could do (as the holders of such a guarantee) to overcome this? Namely so we could follow the principles of open-science AND make sure the value of such a guarantee is not overstated, so that anyone working on a careful human proof / digest is not put off by a public version - nor anyone wanting to work on it in the future? Or do we think this is impossible?

We'd need a better version of arxiv/openreview. It would have to track artefacts, write ups, and supplementary/expository follow-ups separately and provide dois and review comments for them (in a way that filters for spam). We would need dblp / google scholar to track this. We would need a system of tags for such contributions.

And it would have to be community owned in the strongest legal sense (think dblp). I personally believe artefacts matter and ought to count separately and since this year DBLP seems to agree with me on this.

What would be the difference between this and a 1-page paper on the arXiv of the form:

"Just a formalization of the proof of ...."

with

  • a description of the problem
  • link to the github
  • a statement that we welcome future work into digests of this proof, and we think they should get the credit etc....

Not saying I am advocating this, just want to understand the difference.

Edit: Maybe even we could make it anonymous (as much as possible).

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

  • a statement that we welcome future work into digests of this proof, and we think they should get the credit etc....

Well to me the problem with this approach is that you can make this statement yes, but it will not magically make people work on a digestion of the proof, nor will it generate credit to their work. And you might very well still be overtaking people who are currently doing this work.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

What would be the difference between this and a 1-page paper on the arXiv of the form:

"Just a formalization of the proof of ...."

with

  • a description of the problem
  • link to the github
  • a statement that we welcome future work into digests of this proof, and we think they should get the credit etc....

Not saying I am advocating this, just want to understand the difference.

Edit: Maybe even we could make it anonymous (as much as possible).

you’d have to write the pdf for arxiv and host the artefact elsewhere. Arxiv was designed for a different era where the only thing that mattered was a ps/pdf file in the end. I think with a more modern system you can treat all research artefacts as first class objects with their own doi’s. In turn they can be cited better and reviewed separately.

I think one should be a bit wary that the reason the arxiv is still the place to go is that it has community buy-in and it's still something lots of people check. I think the problem with new systems is that they don't yet have this buy-in. For example, we could put the proof on https://palomar-registry.org/ but this is not something that I think the regular mathematician checks. Any new system needs to have this community buy-in to be successful, and achieving that, I think, is incredibly difficult.
If you think people aren't checking it then one possibility is that you dump it there and then try and understand it better, and write a paper iff you succeed.

I think we are in a state of sufficient flux for a new system to gain buy-in as long as its terms are as good as arxiv's and it has better features. This means, being community-owned and run and not charging for hosting preprints

For my current experiments with agents, for every component of a project I have the agent produce a Lean proof, an Explain.md file which explains what it did for that component, a Summary.md file which gives highlights, a SLides.tex file which I can use to present the details of the component, some information which accounts for references and libraries used in deriving the result, and some ancillary files to help with wiring this component into the current project and future projects. The results aren't great, but since I understand the whole project I can easily amend these files (which are a good first draft) into artifacts for use by others. I encourage you to have agents do something similar involving the proof of this open conjecture (if you have access to enough of the original audit trail). You can then take this and educate yourself and others. If the explanations are still too technical, ask for both agent and human help in revising the explanations.

For a full audit, someone will a) have to line up the explanations with the original code, or b) dump the original code and build new code using the explanations. These additional files may never see the public light of day, but the researchers can use them and make them available to other researchers to improve the understanding of the original result from the agent.
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

content:
I would be happy if I saw that someone (1) posted the leanslop to GitHub with an llmslop PDF, (2) a very big header on the README to the effect of "AIs produced a proof of this-and-this conjecture, released here. In the interest of advancing math more productively, we will avoid calling the problem 'DONE' unless at least one human deeply understands the proof and has produced informed thoughts about what does or doesn't generalize, what are the most important insights, etc. We [optional list of names] are currently working on this and aim to release a human-produced and human-friendly paper on the matter by [date]." (3) And they follow through on that.

Optional:

  • A note that someone well versed in the problem and with desire to contribute to the digestion could email some address if they think they might be helpful and want to collaborate on the paper. I think this would be sensibly respected by maybe people but also likely to invite cranks and AI slop
  • Some decision that if you don't get something by a particular date, you release what you have
  • Some mention of what kind of detail on the prompt, what model, etc

Don't mean this to be "I believe this is the only correct way to handle it" or even necessarily "I believe this is the best", just one option to consider that I think I would be happy with if I saw something like it becoming more common.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

It is also worth saying that I think this community is actively prompting releasing these sorts of proofs publicly with things like palomar.

The community is far from being unanimous... What about adding a poll?

This is one of the matters we don't necessarily need to unanimous, we could simply agree to disagree and let the diverse opinions expressed in this topic, to help people in similar situations to make an informed choice.

As for Palomar, lean-eval, Tau Ceti etc., they are infrastructures to facilitate people to do what they decide to do.

For example, people may realize that the formalization they obtained is not new math but heavy machinery on existing techniques, and proving a vast body of reusable math, then decide to make it open, and proceed to contribute to Tau Ceti roadmaps, to participate in coordinated efforts instead of letting duplications pile and rot.

I wonder if part of the problem here is one of terminology: Historically we have used the word 'proof' (in mathematics) to mean something very specific: A human written, and a human readable convincing argument that something is true. This is the only possibility that existed for a long time.

The combination of Lean + AI has opened a new possibility, knowledge that something is true in a way which is both not human written nor human readable. But we are using the same word "proof" to describe this. I think this naturally causes unease in people, because these new "proofs" don't fall into the same category as the traditional proofs we are use to. But those producing such a proof, don't have another name to call it to distinguish it from said traditional proofs.

We have the new word "digest" to describe a new activity; which is understanding these new-style proofs. But IMO this is not quite as useful as having a new name for these new types of proofs.
It seems like another good time to mention Bill Thurston's essay https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9404236

Indulging myself and taking this a bit further, and using the word "warrant" for a place holder for such a new term. One could view there being two boundaries to mathematics now. The human boundary, and the AI boundary made possible with Lean. The human boundary is progressed forward by developing proofs, the AI boundary should be progressed forward by finding 'warrants'. My mental model of the split between human and AI boundaries, is mostly inspired by Tao's mathstodon post here. My takeaway was:

Prematurely producing the final ansatz and thence the solution (by AI), naturally inhibits what human mathematicians may learn from the process and develop for the field. The damages and ramifications to our civilization are far deeper than we may realize today.

There is an X thread by David Louapre after reading Tao's thoughts depicting the larger world explored by human mathematicians, versus the route informed by AI proofs (see attached snapshots too).

Pursuing this line of thought, I had reached the conclusion that AI-informed proofs, by inhibiting the explorations of the unknown, may stop or delay our civilization to learn about how to reach beyond the AI boundary, causing our species to degenerate in overall intelligence, eventually our extinction. A contemporary case study of such effects to the vitality of the ecosystem is Go.

Note that the failure patterns in AI CoTs are not disclosed along with the correct proof, nor that they would be actively preserved and effectively studied internally, because there is no signal or reward on what might be useful or simply beautiful, unlike when being observed by a human mind that proposed that (wrong) ansatz in the first place. This reasoning turned me into an "anti/embrace-digestion" person. :joy:

I think it is worth carefully acknowledging that we're never going to be able to stop people from using AI to find the proofs of results. Even if, as a whole community, we decide such an activity is bad, the fact that it is possible and it is so easy to do nowadays means that people will do it. We should also be careful to not necessarily put a bad stigma around it, because I think in this case people would just hide the fact that they used AI, which I suspect in many cases people are already doing

What we can do is change the dialogue and the discussion around those sorts of activities, and I think, by giving them a different name, we can signal this in the clearest possible way.

In the case of the unit distance conjecture, OpenAI released Rewritten Chain of Thought for the Solution to the Unit Distance Problem per request, which facilitated the digestion. The failure patterns were also requested (allegedly) but eventually not disclosed. （EDIT: If it is going to be the case for most future AI math work, we would have a great deal of opportunities to lose in the process.)

Having thought a lot about this over the last couple of days, I thought I'd put something together which summarizes my current thoughts on this. This includes ideas  which have been given to me, both here publicly and privately, on this topic. I'm framing this from the point of view of a spectator in this rather than somebody in the actual situation, because that was an easier way for me to write it. 

So an AI (under your guidance) has shown an open conjecture is true or false using Lean. Let's start by saying what this is. This is an advancement in human understanding and in human knowledge. Now, let's say what it isn't: it isn't a proof of that result in the traditional sense of the word. That means a human-written and human-readable argument that convinces a human that something is true or not. So here, let's give another word for what you found. A warrant for that conjecture. 

You can think of finding a warrant as similar to digging in your back garden and finding a dinosaur bone. A lot of the time, it requires no expertise and really just a bit of luck that you are digging in the right place and that no one happened to dig there before you. Finding a dinosaur bone obviously doesn't make you qualified to say anything about why the dinosaur was there, what dinosaur it belonged to, the age of the bone, etc. The same holds for finding a warrant. Just because you found a warrant doesn't mean that you have any expertise in the mathematical area where the warrant was found. It doesn't necessarily mean you have any expertise to turn that warrant into a fully fledged proof in the traditional sense. This is essentially what the word "serendipity" describes, and it's a core foundation of scientific progress. 

Of course, you can increase your chances of finding a dinosaur bone by hiring a digger and a dumpster truck to help you move the dirt. Though people may look at you and question why you spent so much money on trying to find dinosaur bones when that money could have been better spent on understanding the bones that we've already got or paying for more experts to find more interesting bones. 

So, with this context in mind and assuming you've already spent that money finding a warrant, what do you do with it? 

I think there isn't a single well-defined answer to this question, but this shouldn't surprise us because there isn't a single well-defined answer to the same question applied to a traditional proof in mathematics. If I come up with a proof of a result in mathematics in the traditional sense, and I ask people what I should do with that proof, I'm going to get differences in answers : Some people will say that you should make it public right away. Some people say you should hold off till it's published in a journal; Some will say you should put it on the arXiv; Some might say it's not even worth that, and you should just put it on a blog post.

The thing that resolves this is two words: "academic judgment.” We put our trust in our fellow colleagues that they are going to make the right decision with regard to this, and this decision is based on experience and community norms. When people break that and go against what would be considered normal academic judgment, their reputation is diminished.

So instead of prescribing something, I think it's worth focusing on what we want the desired outcome to be, and how those desired outcomes are achieved should be up to the individual.

To me, the desired outcome should contain two aspects. Firstly, the warrant of the conjecture should be made public, and the relevant areas of the community should be made aware of his existence. This is taking a kind of purist view that a warrant is mathematical information, and our job should be to increase the mathematical knowledge that humanity has. To not release a warrant and to not make it public seems like a disservice in this respect. It would be great if, every time somebody found a warrant, they also happened to be an expert in the corresponding area and the corresponding mathematics that are used in the proof, so that they could write a human-digestible proof of it. But in most cases, this is not going to be true. To me, the answer to that should not be just to ignore the existence of the warrant, but rather to disseminate the warrant in a way that makes those facts clear. Naturally, in cases where the proof could be understood by those that found the warrant, there is probably going to be some expectation that they write some sort of digest of the proof (or they make some sort of effort to make it accessible for those reading it). But in a lot of cases, these sorts of things will be found by people that really just don't have the expertise in these areas. Even if you have an understanding of the theorem, it's not necessarily true that you'll have an understanding of the underlying mathematics that forms the proof. 

Given that I believe that the warrant of the conjecture should be made public, the second point is to take the social view of mathematics as a discipline rather than just as a body of knowledge. In this viewpoint,the second aspect of the desired outcome is that the dissemination of the warrant of the conjecture does not adversely affect progress towards a traditional proof of that conjecture, nor the resources and credit given to such an endeavour. This requires some social responsibility on those that find the warrants, but again, here the thing at risk is reputation, and we can't stop bad people acting in bad ways. 

So, given those two aspects of a desired outcome, how we achieve them, I think, can be a personal decision (and, again, one that requires academic judgment based on the specifics of the individual cases involved).

I really like the metaphor of finding a dinosaur bone, I think it's a very good one! The "Goodhart's Law" aspect also works there.

A headline that "paleontologists have found the most complete T. Rex skeleton ever" would clearly indicate a good success story for paleontology, but any paleontologist would also tell you that paleontology is not a "find the biggest skeleton" game. As in Joseph's note, there's the job of analyzing the fossil afterwards. But also, there will be other trace fossils (leaf imprints, coprolites, egg shells...) near the skeleton can provide useful secondary learnings, or evidence of new things to find. Finding a lot of isolated bones from many diverse species is useful too: they might not be a big museum-ready story, we might not even know what the dinosaur they're part of looks like, but it helps fill in other parts of the picture. And, crucially, someone who hires a mining team to hunt massive T. Rex skeletons will miss/toss out isolated bones as uninteresting, and they will certainly damage other trace fossils in the process.

It might not be as obvious to non-mathematicians how hunting for a proof with AI could "damage" the soil the way that destructive digging can, but it certainly does stand that risk!

Joseph the usual path is normally the opposite of the one you have followed: first, you would look for a way to prove the conjecture using arguments in a human-comprehensible language, and then, if anything, you would formalize it in Lean. The problem with doing it the other way around (just as OpenAI has done and is currently the trend) is that the process of going from Lean to 'humanly understandable' is infinitely more complex because the Lean code generated by an AI is like an operating system's executable binary, only machines understand it.

In other words, what all the people and companies doing 1) Lean code 2) translating Lean are actually doing is something similar to reverse-engineering a program for which you don't have the readable source code. It can help determine whether something is true or if a condition is met, but, and this is absolutely critical, only if 1) the problem statement in Lean correctly expresses what needs to be formalized, and 2) there are no bugs in Lean. That is to say, you are shifting trust from what a human understands to what a machine says. I am not saying that is wrong, but that is the reality.

Even so, I am a firm believer that, whether we like it or not (which is irrelevant from an evolutionary standpoint, since evolution follows other mechanisms), we will just have to adapt somehow to this scenario where Lean arrives before the explanation and comprehension of the proof. In that process, the 'system' (the human race) will balance itself out. If that Lean code that nobody understands allows us to create or improve an algorithm that a human can understand, and we apply it to improve a cancer-curing drug, then I understand that the need to solve the problem will outweigh the need for a process that is 100% aligned with traditional mathematical standards. If that immediate benefit doesn't exist, 'supply and demand' will prevail. What demand is there to know if a certain conjecture is true or not? Do we really care if we understand the generated Lean code? Is it urgent for humanity?...
